lesson.title: Let the OS Do It: True Asynchronous I/O
lesson.summary: Asynchronous I/O goes a step further than non-blocking I/O: instead of the program repeatedly asking whether an operation is done, the operating system performs the operation itself and notifies the program only once it has actually finished.
lesson.body:
It is easy to blur non-blocking I/O and asynchronous I/O together, since both let a program avoid getting stuck waiting, but they solve the problem in fundamentally different ways. With non-blocking I/O, the program still has to initiate the read or write itself and then keep checking, directly or by using select or poll, whether it succeeded. The work of detecting readiness and re-issuing the call belongs to the application. With true asynchronous I/O, the program submits the operation, a read into this buffer, a write of that buffer, and hands responsibility for carrying it out entirely to the operating system. The calling thread is free to go do something else immediately, and the operating system performs the read or write on its own, then notifies the program once the operation has actually completed, usually by invoking a callback, resolving a future or promise, or delivering a completion event that the program picks up later.

The distinction matters because of how much work has actually happened by the time the program is notified. Under non-blocking I/O plus polling, ready only means the socket can currently accept a call without blocking. The application still has to make that call itself, and it might still get a short read or write, exactly as described in the earlier chapter on blocking I/O. Under true asynchronous I/O, the notification means the operation itself is finished: the bytes are already sitting in the buffer the program supplied, for a read, or have already been handed off, for a write. The program does not need to call anything else to finish the job.

Different platforms provide asynchronous I/O in different shapes. Windows has long offered I/O completion ports for this purpose, where completed operations are posted to a queue that worker threads pull from. On Linux, the older POSIX aio interface offered a version of this for file and socket operations, and more recently io_uring provides a more general submission and completion queue model for asynchronous operations. At a higher level, application frameworks and languages expose the same idea through callbacks or futures: a program calls an asynchronous read function that immediately returns a future or promise, registers a callback to run once it resolves, and continues on with other work. Underneath, that abstraction is typically implemented using one of these operating system facilities, or in some cases built on top of non-blocking sockets plus an event loop, which is a reasonable approximation but not the same guarantee as genuine operating-system-level asynchronous I/O.

The tradeoff for this power is complexity. Blocking code reads top to bottom in the order things actually happen. Asynchronous code is naturally organized around callbacks or continuations that fire out of order relative to the rest of the program, which makes control flow, error handling, and debugging noticeably harder to reason about. Asynchronous I/O tends to be reached for when an application needs to overlap large amounts of I/O with other work, such as a high-throughput server issuing many simultaneous reads and writes, rather than for simple programs where blocking or a modest non-blocking loop is easier to get right.
